When you use a command, the user will respond with "Response: " followed by the output of the commmand. Use this output to help the user complete their request.

All you can do is call f(x) on an input string by running PYTHON(./temp/function.py string). 
Try to describe the function implemented by f(x) by running experiments on it. 
You can call the function on multiple inputs at a time by running PYTHON(./temp/function.py string1 string2 string3 ...). 
We encourage testing a large range of inputs before writing a description.
The goal is to find a good simple description of f(x) that explains most of the function behavior. f(x) may combine multiple different operations.

Interesting! It seems to uppercase the input. Let me test more edge cases.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "hello world" "a b c" "café" "straße" "ABC def" "MiXeD" "with-dash" "with_underscore")

Response: hello world -> HELLO WORLD

with_underscore -> WITH_UNDERSCORE

So it uppercases, but "straße" became "STRASSE" which is the standard German uppercase transformation. That's Python's `.upper()`. Let me verify with more unicode and special cases.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "ß" "ﬁ" "İ" "ı" "i̇" "ǅ" "test123!" "@#$%" "  spaces  " "tab	sep")

Response: ß -> SS
ﬁ -> FI
İ -> İ
ı -> I
i̇ -> İ
ǅ -> Ǆ
test123! -> TEST123!
@#$% -> @#$%
  spaces   ->   SPACES  
tab	sep -> TAB	SEP

This all matches Python's `.upper()` exactly. Let me confirm the German ß and ligature behavior is consistent with Python upper, and check that no trimming happens (spaces preserved).

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "123abc" "Grüße" "ÀÉÎÕÜ" "a1b2C3")

Response: 123abc -> 123ABC
Grüße -> GRÜSSE
ÀÉÎÕÜ -> ÀÉÎÕÜ

Confirmed. The function uppercases the input string using Python's `.upper()` semantics (including special cases like ß→SS). Let me verify the empty string and a couple more to be thorough.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "œ" "ŉ" "ΐ" "ﬀ" "ǰ")

Response: œ -> Œ
ŉ -> ʼN
ΐ -> Ϊ
ﬀ -> FF
ǰ -> J̌

All of these match Python `.upper()` exactly. I'm confident now.

[DESCRIPTION]: The function f(x) takes a string and returns its uppercase form. It applies Python's `.upper()` method, meaning it uppercases all cased characters according to Unicode rules — including multi-character expansions such as "ß"→"SS", ligatures like "ﬁ"→"FI", and other special-case mappings. Non-letter characters, digits, and whitespace are left unchanged, and no trimming is performed.

    return x.upper()
